summary: This RFC proposes the Reliable Asynchronous Transfer Protocol, which lets two programs communicate reliably over a link so data arrives intact and unaltered. It targets asynchronous serial links. It asked for comments and is historic.

eli5.summary: Two people on a noisy phone line repeat anything that was garbled until both are sure the message was heard right.

questions: what is the reliable asynchronous transfer protocol
how does ratp handle noisy serial links
subtitle: A small stop-and-wait protocol that makes noisy serial lines carry data reliably.

tldr.problem: Personal computers talk over RS-232 links and telephone modems, where noise can corrupt bytes or insert spurious ones. Existing serial protocols were one-way, used fixed packet sizes or were too complex.
tldr.mechanism: RATP frames each packet with a one-octet SYNCH pattern, protects the header and the data with checksums, numbers packets with a single bit, and keeps one packet outstanding at a time, resending until it is acknowledged.
tldr.outcome: Data that arrives is meant to arrive intact and unaltered, with a simple enough design for small computers and stand-alone devices. The RFC's status is Historic.

today: RFC 916 has the status Historic. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text itself was a proposal that asked for discussion and suggestions for improvements.

sections.title: Why a New Serial Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 916 specifies the Reliable Asynchronous Transfer Protocol (RATP). It lets two programs communicate over a full-duplex point-to-point link so that data entering one end, if received, arrives at the other end intact and unaltered. It is tailored to RS-232 links, where telephone circuits can insert noise or spurious bytes into the data stream.

The author weighs reliability first and simplicity of implementation second. Dynamic window management is left out, only one packet may be outstanding at a time, and data queued when a connection is closed remotely is discarded. This removes two states from the protocol.

The RFC surveys other serial protocols in an appendix and finds gaps. DDCMP has long headers and a hard-to-compute CRC. The MODEM protocol is one-way and uses a fixed 128-octet block. KERMIT limits packets to 96 octets and does not handle both sides opening at once. RATP lets the receiver state, at connection start, the largest packet it will accept.
sections.eli5: Phone lines are crackly, so the bytes your computer sends can get scrambled. This protocol is a set of simple rules so both sides can tell and fix the damage.

sections.title: Packets, Headers and Checksums
sections.content:
Data is split into 8-bit octets and gathered into packets. Each packet has a four-octet header followed by an optional data portion. The header starts with a SYNCH octet, hex 01 (the ASCII start-of-header character), so a receiver can throw away noise that arrives before a packet. Then come a control octet, a length octet and a header checksum.

The control octet holds the flags SYN, ACK, RST, FIN, EOR and SO, plus two one-bit numbers, SN (sequence number) and AN (acknowledge number). The last bit is reserved and must be zero. EOR marks the end of a higher-level record. SO (single octet) puts one data octet in the length field itself, which saves three octets and is aimed at keyboard characters sent one at a time.

In a SYN packet the length field carries the MDL, the largest number of data octets the other side may send in one packet, at most 255. In other packets it is the data length. The 8-bit header checksum covers the control and length octets, not the SYNCH pattern.

If data is present, it is followed by a 16-bit checksum computed as a one's complement sum like the IP and TCP checksums. The largest possible packet is 261 octets.

Sequence and acknowledge numbers are a single bit each, because only one packet is outstanding per direction. A packet with an unexpected SN is treated as a duplicate and answered with an acknowledgment. Each side may send data whenever its last packet needing a response has been acknowledged, and an acknowledgment can ride on a data packet.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a special start mark, then a little label saying what kind of message it is and how long, and a check number. Another check number at the end shows whether the contents got scrambled.

sections.title: Opening and Closing a Connection
sections.content:
A connection opens with a three-way handshake. One side sends SYN with its initial sequence number and its MDL. The other side, listening, replies with SYN,ACK and its own MDL. The first side then sends an ACK, optionally with the first data. No data may travel before the sender is in the ESTABLISHED state, because the length field carries the MDL during opening.

If both ends open at the same time, both cycle from CLOSED through SYN-SENT and SYN-RECEIVED to ESTABLISHED. If one end crashes and later tries a new connection, the other end sends a reset with RST,ACK and the attempt is refused.

Either side closes by sending a packet with FIN set and no data. The other side answers FIN,ACK, and the first side sends a final ACK and waits in TIME-WAIT for 2*SRTT before closing. Unsent data is reported to the user as a warning.
sections.eli5: Opening is like a phone call: 'Hello?', 'Hello, I can hear you', 'Great, I can hear you too'. Hanging up works the same way, with both sides saying goodbye.

sections.title: States, Packet Reception and Timers
sections.content:
The behavior is described as a state machine. The states are LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT, LAST-ACK, CLOSING, TIME-WAIT and the fictional CLOSED. The user calls are OPEN, SEND, RECEIVE, ABORT, STATUS and CLOSE. The RFC borrows the idea of a Transmission Control Block from TCP.

A receiver reads octets and discards them until it sees SYNCH, reads the three remaining header octets and tests the header checksum. If the header is bad it assumes the SYNCH was noise and starts looking again from the octet after it. If the header is good and the packet carries data, it reads the data plus its two checksum octets and discards the packet if the data checksum fails.

There are three timers. The user timeout bounds opening, acknowledgment and closing, so a cut line does not cause endless retransmission. The retransmission timeout resends any unacknowledged packet, and the connection is aborted after too many retries. The TIME-WAIT timeout should be at least 2*SRTT.
sections.eli5: Each side always knows which step of the conversation it is on, like 'waiting for an answer' or 'saying goodbye'. Timers act like an alarm clock: if no reply comes in time, speak again or give up.

sections.title: Handling Noise and Lost Data
sections.content:
RS-232 frames only single octets, and RATP chooses not to mark the end of a packet. Instead it relies on the length octet, and it protects that octet with the header checksum. If the header fails, the receiver rescans for the next SYNCH, and the sender's retransmission eventually delivers a new copy. This costs nothing unless errors occur.

Lost or corrupted packets are retransmitted after a timeout. The RFC gives an example of calculating it from a smoothed round trip time: SRTT = (ALPHA * SRTT) + ((1- ALPHA) * RTT), with the timeout clamped between a lower and an upper bound (for example 1 second and 1 minute). A fixed realistic upper bound also works, with a lower transmission rate. Duplicates are discarded and the last acknowledgment is resent.

RATP ignores outside flow control characters such as Ctrl-S and Ctrl-Q. Any part of a packet that is dropped looks like a transmission error, which the checksums and retransmission already handle. The sender should choose a maximum data length small enough that flow control rarely triggers. A packet longer than the receiver's MDL is a protocol violation: the receiver sends a reset and the connection is aborted.
sections.eli5: If a piece of the message gets garbled, the receiver just stays quiet. The sender waits a bit, notices no answer, and sends the same message again.

sections.title: Links That Cannot Carry 8 Bits
sections.content:
Some older systems cannot send full 8-bit data over RS-232 and allow only restricted 7-bit communication. For them RATP uses 4/8 packing. Each octet is split into two 4-bit nibbles, high nibble first. The high nibble is sent as a printable ASCII character with @ added, giving characters @ through O. The low nibble is sent with 0 added, giving 0 through ?.

A two-state machine rebuilds octets and discards characters outside the legal range, so a dropped character cannot leave the stream shifted permanently. A listener that can do both formats tries to read incoming data both ways at once, and the first valid header decides the format for the life of the connection. A smart machine that gets no answer in 8-bit mode retries in 4/8 packing, which doubles the time to connect.
sections.eli5: If a phone line can only carry small words, each big word is chopped into two little pieces and glued back together on the other end.

fields.name: Synch Leader
fields.desc: Marks the start of a packet; the ASCII start-of-header character.

fields.name: Control
fields.desc: Flags SYN, ACK, RST, FIN, EOR and SO, plus the SN and AN bits.

fields.name: Data length
fields.desc: Count of data octets, or the MDL in a SYN packet, or the data itself when SO is set.

fields.name: Header Checksum
fields.desc: 8-bit end-around carry checksum over the control and length octets.

messages.label: SN=0 SYN MDL=n
messages.note: Side A opens actively and moves to SYN-SENT.

messages.label: SN=0 AN=1 SYN,ACK MDL=m
messages.note: Side B was listening; it moves to SYN-RECEIVED.

messages.label: SN=1 AN=1 ACK + DATA
messages.note: Side A is ESTABLISHED; B is ESTABLISHED on receipt.
